articles.title: In 2021, a Polish recycler laid retired wind-turbine blades across the Szprotawa River; the former power equipment became a bridge for pedestrians and cyclists
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how a retired wind-turbine blade transformed into a pedestrian bridge over the Szprotawa River in Poland, showcasing innovative recycling and engineering solutions.
articles.body: A retired wind-turbine blade became the main structural element of a pedestrian and cycling bridge over Poland's Szprotawa River in 2021. The project was developed in the town of Szprotawa by Anmet, which is a local company working with the Rzeszów University of Technology on ways to reuse composite wind-turbine components. The bridge was built after residents had lacked a convenient pedestrian crossing at the location for a long time, and engineers incorporated it into a new crossing that connected parts of the town that were separated by the river instead of sending the used blade to disposal. The Szprotawa municipal government reported in December 2021 that construction of the pedestrian and cycling route had been completed and that the new bridge had been built using a wind-turbine blade.From turbine equipment to bridge structureAnmet's account of the project says the footbridge was built on October 21, 2021, in Szprotawa and was the first structure of its type produced by the company. The firm says the project followed three years of research and development carried out with the Rzeszów University of Technology.Wind-turbine blades are difficult to recycle in the same way as metals, as they are generally made from composite materials, including fiberglass and resin, that are engineered to remain strong and lightweight during years of operation. Separating those materials for conventional recycling can be difficult once a blade reaches the end of its service life.That has encouraged engineers and researchers to look at ways of keeping the blades intact and finding new structural uses for them, and the Szprotawa project took exactly that approach. The engineers retained its structural properties and incorporated it into a bridge rather than breaking the blade down into smaller materials. The blade formed the central structural element, while a seating area was incorporated into the middle of the bridge.A local transport problem shaped the projectSzprotawa's municipal government said that the crossing was intended to improve pedestrian and bicycle movement between the eastern and northern parts of the town, and connect streets and recreational areas on opposite sides of the river. A pedestrian and cycling route was built alongside the river, and the municipality added lighting powered by photovoltaic panels. The completed route linked the river crossing with nearby recreational infrastructure and a canoe landing.The municipality put the total value of the project at 245,000 Polish złoty, with 80,000 złoty coming from a regional tourism infrastructure program. The crossing was initially scheduled to open at the beginning of January 2022, although the bridge itself had been constructed in 2021.The blade became part of the bridge's identityThe project was subsequently presented as an example of repurposing composite turbine components rather than treating them only as waste. A Polish construction competition listing for the project describes the Szprotawa bridge as the first bridge of its type and says its main structural components were retired wind-turbine blades.The engineering question was whether a blade that is designed to withstand years of aerodynamic loading could be adapted to carry loads in a bridge. According to the competition record, testing was carried out to establish the strength and stiffness of the composite blade as a bridge girder.That changed the role of the old turbine component, as it was no longer part of a machine designed to generate electricity, but a structural member in a public crossing. The town's bridge remains a pedestrian and cycling connection, while the retired blade has become part of the infrastructure it was used to create.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sweden heads to the polls: What’s at stake in the knife-edge election?
articles.summary: Sweden votes on Sunday as voters weigh migration, crime, the economy and whether the far right will enter government.
articles.body:
Stockholm, Sweden – On Sunday, Swedes will vote in a knife-edge general election that could see it either usher in a left-wing coalition or take a step even further to the right and welcome the Sweden Democrats , a party with neo-Nazi roots, into government for the first time.

Once a political pariah, the party has become the greatest force on the right and has already helped shape government policy from beyond the cabinet. Now, Moderate Party leader and Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson wants to bring it formally into power.

Opposing them is a centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson, which has been leading in the polls, although the gap has been narrowing in recent weeks.

Sweden’s four left-bloc parties now have support of between 49.3 and 50.8 percent, according to the surveys conducted by the Ipsos, Demoskop and Indikator Opinion polling firms, while support for the coalition government and the Sweden Democrats stands at 47.6 to 49 percent, according to polls released by Swedish Radio and dailies Aftonbladet and DN.

Advance voting has been running since August 26.

Sunday, however, is the official election day when polling stations will open at 8am (06:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (18:00 GMT).

Swedes are voting in three elections on the same day: one for members of the national parliament, one for the regional council and one for the municipal council.

How are Sweden’s political parties distributed?

On the right are the governing Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, as well as the Sweden Democrats, who have propped up the government from outside since all four parties signed an agreement in 2022.

On the left are the Social Democrats, the Left Party and the Greens, with the Centre Party a possible fourth.

Swedish politics has traditionally been built around coalition-building, compromise and minority governments rather than one party winning outright.

Governments do not need a majority of seats to take office, but they won’t survive in parliament unless smaller parties form agreements within blocs.

What are the key issues for this election?

A number of issues are on voters’ minds ahead of this election.

Immigration remains one of the defining issues in Swedish politics, and a major reason the Sweden Democrats have gone from political pariah to kingmakers.

Analysts say the 2015 refugee crisis, when an estimated 1.3 million asylum seekers arrived in Europe, handed the party a major opportunity.

In Sweden alone, 163,000 arrived – the highest annual figure in the country’s history and the largest per capita intake in the European Union.

According to Sweden’s annual SOM (society, opinion and media) survey, immigration became the single most important issue for 53 percent of Swedish voters almost overnight that year.

As a result, Sweden has dramatically tightened its migration policy since the crisis, with asylum numbers now far below their peak.

The government has introduced tougher residency and citizenship rules and, this year, began offering migrants with residency permits about $36,000 as an incentive to leave.

The Sweden Democrats want to go further, while the centre left has also moved towards a more restrictive position than it once held.

The argument is now less about whether migration should be reduced and more about what integration should look like.

However, some of the most hardline new migration policies introduced have gone “too far” even for right-wing voters, Zina al-Dewany, a political commentator and editorial writer for the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, told Al Jazeera.

The government’s focus on repatriation and hubris, driven by the upswell of support for tougher measures in the country, led to overreach and a spate of scandals that dominated Swedish headlines this year, she said.

This largely centred around a wave of deportation orders issued to teenagers who had grown up in Sweden and were being told to leave on turning 18 while their parents stayed – a practice the government ultimately suspended in March and moved to reform in June.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has transformed Sweden’s security policy, helping drive its historic decision to join NATO in 2024.

Sweden has provided about $16.4bn in military and civilian support to Ukraine since 2022.

There is unusually broad agreement across the political spectrum that Sweden should continue backing Ukraine, with debate focused less on whether to support Ukraine than on how much Sweden should spend and how far Europe should go in strengthening its own defence.

On Palestine , the debate is very different.

The current right-wing government does not regard Israel’s conduct in Gaza as genocide and has not joined South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

However, it has pushed for EU sanctions against “extremist” settlers and ministers, and in April proposed extra tariffs and export certificates on settlement products.

If the Sweden Democrats were to get into government, it would represent the most pro-Israel views in the bloc.

Its motions this session have called for moving the Swedish embassy to Jerusalem and ending all Swedish aid to Palestinians.

Its leader, Jimmie Akesson, said in January that, if it were up to him, he would absolutely withdraw Sweden’s recognition of Palestine.

The left bloc is aligned on several key issues, including resuming funding to UNRWA, which has been accused by Israel of having links with Hamas, but which provides the majority of humanitarian support to Palestinians.

The Left Party and Green Party have called for Sweden to join South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the ICJ.

“If the left bloc comes to power, you will see a trade boycott of Israel, more money to UNRWA, and we want more funding to the ICC,” Anfal Mahdi, an opposition councillor in Malmo for the Left Party, told Al Jazeera, referring to the International Criminal Court, which issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 on suspicion of committing war crimes.

Gang violence has become a focus of Sweden’s political debate over the past decade.

With a population of 10.6 million, Sweden has one of Europe’s highest rates of deadly gun violence. The government has responded with tougher sentences, more police resources and measures targeting criminal networks.

There are signs the crackdown is working: shootings and deaths have fallen sharply this year compared with 2022.

But friction remains about how to deal with the issue, with the right saying the progress proves its approach is working, while the left argues that prevention, schools and social services are equally important.

After years of rising inflation and a prolonged economic downturn, the cost of living is a major concern for voters.

The parties are competing over how to put more money in people’s pockets – through tax cuts, more benefits or levels of public spending.

The right has emphasised lower taxes and incentives to work, while the centre-left is promising investment in welfare and household finances.

Healthcare consistently ranks among the issues Swedish voters value most.

That makes it politically important even though much of the responsibility for providing it lies with Sweden’s regions rather than the national government.

The parties are debating waiting times, staffing and access to care, as well as how Sweden should fund its welfare state.

The centre left is campaigning heavily on investment in healthcare, schools and other public services, while the right argues that stronger incentives to work and economic growth are needed to sustain them.

articles.title: China rejects Anthropic allegations of using Claude to train their models
articles.summary: China News: China has firmly rejected accusations by US artificial intelligence company Anthropic that Chinese AI labs, including DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot A.
articles.body: China has firmly rejected accusations by US artificial intelligence company Anthropic that Chinese AI labs, including DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot AI, carried out large-scale efforts to extract responses from its Claude models and use them to train their own systems.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing “advocates AI for good” and accused Anthropic of “distorting facts”.“We firmly oppose attempts to throw mud at China by distorting facts,” Mao said at a regular news conference on Friday.The comments came a day after Anthropic released a threat intelligence report alleging that several China-based AI companies had conducted what it called “illicit distillation” campaigns against Claude.What Anthropic’s report allegesDistillation is a common AI training technique in which a less powerful model learns from the outputs of a more capable model. Anthropic alleged that Chinese AI labs went further by using networks of accounts to systematically send prompts to Claude, collect its responses and use those exchanges to improve their own models.According to the report, the operations involved more than 151 million exchanges with Claude by Alibaba alone between May and July, making it the largest distillation campaign Anthropic said it had measured.The activity peaked at nearly 3 million exchanges a day and involved more than 3,500 accounts that Anthropic described as fraudulent. The company said Alibaba used Claude’s outputs to train its Qwen models and also used the model for wider AI research, including reinforcement learning and model architecture work.Anthropic said some of the exchanges involved sensitive information belonging to individual users, multinational companies and state-affiliated organisations. It said such practices were likely inconsistent with privacy laws and the companies’ own terms of service.Moonshot, DeepSeek accused of similar tacticsAnthropic also accused Beijing-based Moonshot AI of secretly routing Kimi users’ requests to Claude and using some exchanges to train its models. The company said Moonshot relayed nearly 300,000 requests through 5,380 accounts in 10 days and more than 23 million exchanges between May and July. DeepSeek was accused of similar tactics, with Anthropic reporting more than 12 million distillation attacks over 14 days in July. Xiaomi was also named in the report.Anthropic said some unauthorised exchanges exposed sensitive data, including internal CCTV footage from Chengdu. It said it detected and disrupted the alleged operations between December 2025 and August 2026 across seven areas of AI misuse, including cyber operations, surveillance, fraud, weapons development and model distillation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Guatemalan judge clears deputy minister, three leaders of terrorism charges
articles.summary: Luis Pacheco and three other Indigenous ex-leaders cleared of charges over 2023 Guatemala protests.
articles.body:
A Guatemalan court has cleared a deputy minister and three other Indigenous leaders of terrorism charges, brought over their role in leading protests against a prosecutor accused of trying to block President Bernardo Arevalo from taking office.

The Third Criminal Court judge, Mynor Moto, dismissed the case on Friday at the request of prosecutors, who concluded after their own investigation that the four had not broken any laws by organising the protests in October 2023.

The decision adds to the collapse of a prosecution built under former Attorney General Consuelo Porras, who was sanctioned by the United States, the European Union, Canada and other governments over corruption allegations, the persecution of human rights advocates, and efforts to undermine Arevalo’s 2023 election win.

She lost her bid for a third term as attorney general in April, after a judicial commission left her off its shortlist of candidates.

The minister, Luis Pacheco, is deputy minister of sustainable development at Guatemala’s Ministry of Energy and Mines and previously led the 48 Cantones of Totonicapan, a Maya Indigenous authority in the western highlands known for organising protests.

He was prosecuted alongside Hector Chaclan, the group’s former treasurer, Basilio Puac, its former vice president, and Esteban Toc, a former deputy mayor of the Indigenous municipality of Solola, a separate traditional authority that operates alongside the town’s official council.

Prosecutors had accused the four of illicit association, terrorism and obstructing justice, with Puac and Toc also facing sedition charges, over protests demanding Porras resign after she was accused of trying to block Arevalo’s inauguration.

Pacheco had been suspended from his post during the case, and the ministry said it welcomed the ruling and expected him back at work shortly.

The United Nations human rights office said the ruling “reaffirms the freedoms of expression and assembly” and recognises legitimate forms of Indigenous organising, adding that it has documented a wider pattern of criminalising Indigenous leaders in Guatemala.

Arevalo, who took office in 2024 after months of legal challenges from Porras’s office, has made unwinding those prosecutions a priority, appointing a new attorney general who pledged to review cases seen as arbitrarily brought under his predecessor.

articles.title: 9/11 at 25: How the ‘War on Terror’ helped mainstream Europe’s far right
articles.summary: The ‘War on Terror’ gave far-right Islamophobia legitimacy, reach and electoral force.
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, the political order built in their aftermath continues to shape Europe. The Global War on Terror (GWOT) helped far right parties in Europe gain political prominence they had long been denied. Islamophobic narratives that shaped global policy after 2001 legitimised an anti-Muslim racism that had already been building within Europe’s far right for years.

Before September 11, far right parties in Europe had been largely marginalised within the continent’s multi-party systems. Even where some won significant electoral support, many remained politically stigmatised or excluded from power, and were better known for anti-Semitism and open nostalgia for their fascist origins than as credible contenders for government.

But the ground was already shifting before the towers fell. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the far right’s long-standing racism began to sharpen its focus on Islam specifically. Parties such as the French Front National (now the Rassemblement National) and the Austrian Freedom Party discovered Islam as their new “enemy within”: Arabs and Black communities in France became, in far-right rhetoric, simply “Muslims.” So did Turks in Austria. The People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD) was arguing as early as 1991 that Islam posed a threat to liberal democracy and stood in the way of immigrant “integration.” By the late 1990s, Pim Fortuyn had written a book titled Against the Islamisation of Our Culture, introducing a cruder, more overt strain of Islamophobia to Dutch politics.

Then came September 11, which handed the far right an opening it hadn’t had to build for itself.

When 19 al-Qaeda hijackers crashed four planes into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania, killing 2,977 people, President George W. Bush declared a ‘Global War on Terror’. The far right no longer needed to manufacture anti-Muslim sentiment on its own; political speeches, media coverage and wars waged across Muslim-majority countries did much of that work for them.

Bush insisted the fight targeted “terrorists” who had perverted the message of Islam, not Islam itself. But the rhetoric and policy that followed routinely treated all Muslims as suspects, casting the religion itself as inherently violent — a framing that helped mainstream and globalise Islamophobia over the course of the ‘War on Terror’.

Bush’s declaration that “either you are with us or you are with the terrorists” left European governments with little room to manoeuvre. More than 13 European countries joined the US-led invasion of Afghanistan, with British forces most directly engaged in combat. Twelve joined the invasion and occupation of Iraq; the UK and Poland took on major combat roles, while France and Germany, this time, opposed the war.

Blatantly Islamophobic media coverage across the continent accompanied these campaigns, reinforcing an image of the violent, threatening Muslim. Attacks by al-Qaeda affiliates in Madrid and London deepened the sense that the enemy was already “within,” casting suspicion on any Muslim as a potential threat. Meanwhile, European governments — with the far right still largely excluded from power — enacted their own Islamophobic policies: countering violent extremism and deradicalisation programmes, including the UK’s Prevent strategy. They also cooperated in hosting secret CIA ‘black sites’ and facilitating rendition flights to Guantanamo Bay and other torture sites. These programmes rested on the premise that Muslim religious belief was itself a kind of dormant threat, always capable of being “activated” into violence against the West. Guantanamo Bay became the era’s most infamous symbol of this logic — a lawless site where innocent Muslims were shipped and held on unfounded suspicion, without legal grounds.

Self-styled experts on “extremism” and “terrorism” — Pamela Geller, Frank Gaffney, Daniel Pipes, Robert Spencer — built careers legitimising this framework for American audiences and soon forged connections with Europe’s strengthening far-right movements. Together they formed the self-described “Counter-Jihad Movement”, a transatlantic network of anti-Muslim organisations, political parties, writers, bloggers and activists united by the claim that “Western civilisation” is under attack by Islam. Beginning in 2007, the movement used the OSCE’s annual Human Dimension Implementation Meeting to spread its ideology within European and North American policy circles. Far-right leaders from Austria, Belgium, England, the Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, Switzerland and Norway convened at annual counter-jihad conferences held in cities across the continent.

Years before Pamela Geller mobilised against the falsely named “Ground Zero Mosque” in New York in 2010, her European counterparts were already organising transnationally against mosque construction. In 2008, the Cities Against Islamisation initiative brought together far-right leaders from the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Austria, France and Italy, marching alongside anti-Muslim activists from the United States.

Slowly, anti-Muslim mobilisation proved electorally successful. As opposition parties, far-right movements gained ground — first by pressuring mainstream rivals into adopting their rhetoric, then by becoming coalition partners in national governments from Austria to Bulgaria, Hungary, the Netherlands, Italy, Norway, Poland, and Finland. In Denmark and Sweden, they became kingmakers instead, shaping policy from outside the cabinet.

Anti-Muslim policy has only expanded since. Far-right parties, and mainstream governments pressured by them, have passed a growing list of restrictions on Muslims’ religious freedom: bans on the full-face veil in several countries, bans on the hijab for teachers, students, or public employees in others, and severe restrictions — in some places outright bans — on mosque construction. Muslims, who make up a disproportionate share of Europe’s working poor, have been pushed further to the margins as a result.

Even as more Muslims pursue education and professional advancement, a securitised discourse — built on the logic of the GWOT and fused with far-right “great replacement” conspiracy theories — has adapted to meet them. The old accusation that Muslims refuse to integrate has given way to a newer one: that Muslims who succeed pose an even greater risk, secretly working to subvert Western societies. It is the same role historically assigned to Jews — the “enemy within” who can never be trusted.

Several governments have institutionalised this suspicion by targeting Muslim-led civil society organisations. Strict surveillance of mosques and NGOs, paired with curtailed civil liberties, has become standard practice across many European states — framed variously as combating “political Islam” (Austria), “Islamist separatism” (France), or “legalistic Islamism” (Germany). In each case, the tolerated Muslim is the invisible one: the individual who does not claim a seat at the table or protest injustice.

The language and infrastructure built by the ‘Global War on Terror’ allowed all of this to take root and expand largely unchallenged. With much of Europe still unwilling to reckon with its own histories of colonialism, racism and fascism, Islamophobia has become a broadly accepted political position — one the far right did not simply exploit, but actively cultivated into its own success.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In the 1970s, Washington tied thousands of discarded tyres together across 20 Puget Sound reefs to improve bottom fishing; decades later, the ropes failed and more than 100,000 tyres remained underwater
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Washington's 1970s tire reefs aimed to boost fishing have now turned into an environmental hazard, with over 100,000 discarded tires still lying in Puget Sound.
articles.body: Washington's experiment with artificial reefs in Puget Sound began with the practical goal of creating more structure on the seafloor for rockfish, lingcod and other bottom-dwelling fish while expanding recreational fishing opportunities. Discarded vehicle tires, among other materials, were bundled together and lowered into the water at 20 reef sites during the 1970s.A 2025 article from the University of Washington's School of Marine and Environmental Affairs describes the tire reefs as one of Puget Sound's clearest examples of how artificial habitat can produce unintended problems. The tires were tied together with polypropylene rope, and thousands were placed at each of the 20 sites.The reefs were built for bottom fishingThe University of Washington account says new federal laws and court decisions in the 1970s and 1980s tightened restrictions on salmon fishing, which prompted recreational anglers to put more attention on bottom fishing for species such as rockfish and lingcod. Washington's Department of Fish and Wildlife worked with recreational fishing groups as artificial reef construction expanded. Tires were only one of several materials used, while other reefs incorporated concrete, natural rock, plastics, PVC, vessels, barges and even train cars.The basic idea was to add vertical relief and structural complexity to parts of the seabed that provided relatively little cover. Natural rocky reefs provide crevices and surfaces where algae and invertebrates can live, while smaller fish can use the structure for shelter from predators and currents. The polypropylene rope deteriorated, which allowed individual tires and sections of the artificial structures to move away from their original locations. The tires became loose objects on the seafloor and, in some locations, eventually reached shorelines, instead of remaining as stable reef units.A reef material became a cleanup problemThe Washington Department of Natural Resources now considers the old tire structures an environmental problem rather than a successful fish habitat, and its Tire Pile Removal Program says thousands of surplus automotive tires were placed on the bottom of Puget Sound during the 1970s and 1980s to attract native reef fish and improve recreational fishing. The agency says the artificial structures have since been judged unsuccessful and has begun planning and carrying out their removal.DNR began prioritizing removal work in 2019 and has worked with the Washington Department of Ecology, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission and Washington Scuba Alliance to locate and survey the old reefs. DNR's survey work between 2019 and 2021 examined 20 locations using multibeam sonar and underwater video. Tires were found at 14 of those sites, with major differences between locations in the number of tires and the size of the affected areas.The University of Washington report says that the material has weathered and fragmented, while chemical compounds associated with degraded tires can enter the surrounding environment. It also notes that tire surfaces did not provide the same biological communities found on more suitable artificial reef materials.More than 100,000 tires are still being dealt withA March 2025 KING 5 report estimated that more than 100,000 tires remained in Puget Sound from the old reef program, while noting that the exact number is uncertain because not all tire placements are mapped. DNR has identified multiple priority sites, and its work involves locating tire piles, recovering them from the water and sending the damaged material for appropriate disposal.The original reefs were intended to solve a fisheries problem by adding structure to the seabed, and decades later, the same structures have become objects that marine managers are trying to remove. The contrast has also shaped how newer artificial reefs in Puget Sound are designed, with greater attention to durable materials, site selection and long-term maintenance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1983, Atari dumped truckloads of unsold video games in a New Mexico landfill; when the site was excavated in 2014, about 1,300 cartridges were recovered, with some later selling for hundreds or thousands of dollars
articles.summary: US News: In a shocking revelation, Atari buried truckloads of video game cartridges, including the infamous E.T. game, in a New Mexico landfill in 1983. In 2014, over 1,300 cartridges were excavated, with some fetching thousands of dollars at auction, changing the narrative of video game history forever.
articles.body: At a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, in September 1983, Atari disposed of truckloads of video-game cartridges and computer equipment. Among the material were cartridges for E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, the Atari 2600 game that was closely associated with the company’s troubles. More than 30 years later, an excavation at the landfill recovered about 1,300 cartridges, turning a decades-old industry story into tangible evidence. Subsequently, some of the recovered games were auctioned online for hundreds of dollars, whereas E.T. cartridges were sold for more than $1,500.A contemporary report published on September 28, 1983, suggested that the company dumped 14 truckloads of video-game and computer equipment at the landfill in New Mexico. The material allegedly came from Atari’s El Paso, Texas, operation. An Atari spokesperson claimed at the time that the items were simply defective components being discarded. However, this factory-defect explanation clashed with the reality of the situation; the site had actually reportedly become a graveyard for millions of functional, unsold retail returns that the company could no longer afford to store. E.T., Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man were some of the games dumped at the landfill.How E.T. became linked with Atari’s troublesDuring a crucial Christmas shopping season, Atari released its adaptation of Steven Spielberg’s 1982 film for the Atari 2600. According to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, programmer Howard Scott Warshaw was given only five and a half weeks to complete the game. This was significantly less time than a conventional development period of six to nine months. The company also allegedly needed to sell roughly four million cartridges to recover the cost of the licensing deal, but sales fell far short of that target.Atari was already facing much bigger market problems. And the game’s commercial difficulties only made things worse for the company. The Smithsonian account notes that the Atari VCS, later known as the Atari 2600, was facing competition from systems including Mattel’s Intellivision and Coleco’s ColecoVision. Meanwhile, independent publishers were also adding large numbers of games to the market. The resulting video-game crash was not caused by E.T. alone, as the industry’s downturn had several other causes as well.By 1983, Atari had substantial quantities of unnecessary inventory. WIRED’s account of the Alamogordo excavation reported that stores had begun returning unsold products, and that Atari’s El Paso operation was poorly equipped to refurbish or otherwise handle all the returns. The company eventually transported pallets of games and computer equipment from El Paso to Alamogordo, where the landfill was considered less vulnerable to scavengers.The story from a reported dump to a 2014 excavationFor decades, the story became increasingly distorted. During the 2014 excavation, WIRED reported that the original incident had morphed in the public imagination into an urban legend: Atari having buried huge quantities of E.T. cartridges specifically, even though contemporary reporting suggests that multiple Atari games and hardware were involved. This uncertainty over the exact contents helped turn the massive dumping into gaming folklore.Fuel Entertainment took the initiative to settle the mystery in 2013 when it pursued the opportunity to excavate the landfill for a documentary project. Joe Lewandowski, a local garbage contractor, had knowledge of the site's history and helped researchers identify the likely location of the burial. Eventually, the excavation was carried out on 26 April 2014, with filmmakers, archaeologists and other working professionals searching the landfill.Excavators found Atari 2600 cartridges including E.T., Asteroids, Pac-Man and other titles. Atari hardware was also recovered from the site. This served as evidence that the site was a broader Atari disposal area rather than a graveyard devoted exclusively to one game. The City of Alamogordo subsequently reported that approximately 1,300 cartridges had been recovered, and in September 2014, the city voted to auction 800 of them. The recovered games were considered valuable, particularly because their archaeological provenance could be documented.When landfill debris turned into collectable historyAlmost immediately after the excavation, the transformation from discarded inventory to collectable had begun. In November 2014, the Tularosa Basin Historical Society put around 100 recovered games up for auction on eBay. This included E.T., Centipede and Defender as well. Reports from various sources claimed that the auctions started between $50 and $100, while a particularly desirable E.T. cartridge had already attracted bids exceeding $400 before the auctions closed. Each of the games came with a certificate of authenticity linking it to the Alamogordo excavation.In August 2015, Ars Technica reported that 881 recovered Atari cartridges sold for a combined $107,930.15 in a series of eBay auctions. The City of Alamogordo received about $65,000 from the total sales, while the Tularosa Basin Historical Society also received a share. The most expensive cartridge in that sale was an E.T. copy that fetched $1,535.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2013, Leonardo DiCaprio’s foundation gave $3 million to Nepal’s tiger effort; the country’s count later climbed from 121 animals to 355
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation's $3 million grant boosted Nepal's tiger conservation efforts leading to a remarkable increase from 121 to 355 tigers by 2022.
articles.body: In November 2013, for a tiger-conservation programme in Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape, the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation awarded $3 million to WWF. The objective was to help the country double its wild tiger population by 2022 from its 2009 baseline estimate of 121 tigers. The grant was designed to strengthen anti-poaching patrols, protect core breeding areas, restore wildlife corridors and improve tiger monitoring. Nearly a decade later, Nepal’s national tiger survey estimated 355 wild tigers in 2022, compared with 121 in the country’s 2009 nationwide estimate. The increase was larger than the tiger estimate that would have represented a doubling of the original population.Nepal’s official Tiger Conservation Action Plan records national estimates of 121 tigers in 2009, 198 in 2013, 235 in 2018, and 355 in 2022. This paints a picture that recovery was already underway when the DiCaprio Foundation announced its donation in 2013. The timing of the grant is still significant. In 2010, governments from the world’s tiger-range countries committed to the global Tx2 goal. The aim was to double the number of wild tigers by 2022. Subsequently, Nepal emerged as one of the countries with a realistic chance of achieving the target set.The goal behind the $3 million grant in 2013The Terai Arc Landscape was a difficult conservation challenge. The region contained protected areas that were important not just for tigers but also for rhinoceroses and elephants. Millions of people also depended on the wider landscape for their livelihoods. The area covered around 9,000 square miles and was reported to be home to seven million people. This high density of human and animal populations indicated that protecting tigers required solutions far beyond simply guarding national park boundaries. Recogising this, the World Wide Fund (WWF) actively designed initiatives to establish financial safety nets for local communities.When the grant was announced, the global conservation organisation said that DiCaprio Foundation’s funding would be used to strengthen anti-poaching work through improved ranger patrols, monitoring technology, community policing and intelligence gathering. Additional guard posts and efforts to strengthen corridors connecting protected areas were also reported to be supported by the grant.The programme also included measures to reduce conflicts that can arise when humans and large carnivores share the same landscape. To accomplish this, the grant helped establish community-managed insurance funds to compensate families for livestock losses caused by predators. It reportedly aimed to help create income-generating activities associated with tourism, handicrafts and organic vegetable production.The rise from 198 tigers in 2013 to 355 in 2022Nepal’s next national assessment after 2013 came in 2018. The estimated tiger population in that assessment had reached 235. WWF’s reporting at the time underscored that this number represented a near-doubling of the 121-tiger baseline from 2009. The 2018 result indicated that the upward trend had continued beyond the initial years of the Tx2 programme.Nepal’s Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, alongside other partner organisations, conducted a nationwide tiger and prey survey covering 18,928 square kilometres in 2022. Researchers used camera traps and distinctive stripe patterns of individual tigers to identify animals and estimate populations across the country’s major tiger habitats. The resulting estimate was 355. The survey recorded 128 tigers in the Chitwan landscape, 125 in Bardia, 41 in Parsa, 25 in Banke and 36 in Shuklaphanta.The rise was described as an increase of about 193% from the 2009 baseline. The result also reflected the importance of protecting core habitats and corridors, working with local communities and intensifying action against poaching and illegal wildlife trade.A recovery built over more than one decadeThe increase cannot be credited to a single grant, organisation or intervention. Nepal’s government led the national surveys and implemented tiger-protection measures, while WWF, the National Trust for Nature Conservation, the Zoological Society of London and other partners provided technical, financial and conservation support.The country’s own conservation strategy points to the importance of maintaining protected habitats while securing corridors outside formal parks. Its 2013 national survey had shown tigers’ presence in forests and corridors beyond protected areas. They identified the need to maintain connectivity between different tiger populations and worked on it together.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: By 2023, a Washington State entrepreneur had developed a credit system for fashion brands to fund textile recovery; the system was processing about 50 tonnes of textile waste a month
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Clarabeth Concaret's Fabricure is transforming the fashion industry by turning textile waste into a currency, facilitating 50 tonnes of recovery monthly across multiple nations.
articles.body: Once clothes are damaged, unsold or discarded, they can become difficult to reuse, particularly when different fibres, dyes and blends are mixed. A Washington State entrepreneur was trying to change that by assigning textile waste a financial value. According to UNICEF Innovation, Clarabeth Concaret, who was born and raised on Orcas Island in Washington State, developed Fabricure around the idea of fabric credits. The model was inspired by carbon and plastic credits: fashion brands could purchase credits corresponding to the amount of textile waste they generated, with the money channelled into textile recovery and recycling projects. By November 2023, UNICEF reported that Fabricure was processing about 50 tons of textile waste a month across Ghana, Togo, Kenya and Chile.Giving textile waste a priceTextile waste is difficult to manage because garments can contain different fibres and blends, making identification and processing more complicated. Research published in the Journal of Cleaner Production examined the use of infrared spectroscopy and automatic classification to identify different types of post-consumer textile waste, highlighting the role that improved sorting technologies could play in recovering discarded fibres. Fabricure's approach was to add a financial mechanism to this wider waste-recovery challenge. Instead of requiring every fashion company to establish its own recycling infrastructure, the credit system allowed brands to finance textile recovery projects in places where discarded clothing was already accumulating.This distinction mattered as a Fabric Credit was more than just a voucher for returning a specific item of clothing. Fabricure states that one credit equals 1 kg of textile waste that would otherwise have ended up in a dump or been incinerated. Brands could then buy credits based on the amount of waste they produced, matching Fabricure’s supply-chain interventions. By 2023, the model started to be piloted outside the USA. UNICEF claimed that Ghana, Togo, Kenya, and Chile were the nations receiving support from Fabricure, with women-led recycling partners playing key roles in its implementation. It was also reported by the company that three major brands were collaborating with the firm on neutral fabric collections.What happens after the clothes are collected?According to Forest Valley Institute, the Fabricure co-founder Payton McGriff and Concaret saw recycling and upcycling initiatives that were capable of reducing waste but depended heavily on grants or charitable funding. The credit model was designed to create a commercial source of revenue for such projects. Fabricure’s current model involves collecting material from landfills or other waste sites, sorting it by fibre type and weight, and then sending it to recycling partners equipped to handle different materials. The recovered textiles can then be used in different ways rather than following a single recycling route.Fabricure's work with Eco2librium in Kenya provides an example of how this approach could be applied on the ground. Fabricure says a pilot launched in autumn 2023 aimed to divert 7.5 tonnes of textiles from Kenyan landfills, while investigating whether cellulose-based textile waste could be used as compost for agricultural soils. The project therefore connected textile recovery with an environmental problem of declining soil quality. This was part of a broader effort by Fabricure to explore different uses for recovered material.Can credits change fashion's waste problem?Paying for waste recovery does not, on its own, make the fashion industry circular. Fabricure's approach recognises that reducing the amount of fabric used, the number of clothes produced and overall consumption should come first, with recovery dealing with the waste that is left behind. The credit system works at this later stage. It puts a financial value on discarded textiles and directs money towards projects that can collect and process them, rather than asking every fashion company to build its own recycling system.This approach could become more important as governments and consumers put greater pressure on fashion brands to take responsibility for the waste they generate. According to Concaret, the idea was to put a price on textile recovery and give brands a way to support waste-recovery projects. In 2023, Fabricure said it was processing tens of tonnes of textile waste each month, suggesting that the system was already being used beyond the pilot stage.But credits alone cannot solve fashion's waste problem. If brands use them simply to balance out the waste created by producing more clothes, they could allow the industry to carry on with the same pattern of consumption. Their role could be more useful if the money helps recover, recycle and reuse textiles that would otherwise be thrown away. In the end, the real measure of the system is not just how much waste it recovers, but whether it also forms part of a wider effort to produce and throw away less clothing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: What did US intelligence know before the 9/11 attacks?
articles.summary: The CIA have declassified documents showing US presidents were warned about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda before 9/11.
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, the CIA has released a series of presidential briefing documents showing what United States leaders had been told about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda in the years before the plane hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe called the release of the documents “an act of exceptional transparency”. This is the agency’s largest-ever release of presidential daily briefs, the classified intelligence summaries written for the president and his most senior officials.

The files cover the period from February 1998 to September 12, 2001 – the day after the deadly attacks on New York City and Washington, DC – and reveal how the CIA tracked bin Laden’s movements, his financing and his networks inside the US and abroad.

In one, a briefer warns that the group behind that year’s East Africa embassy bombings “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.

Another notes that some in bin Laden’s network had received hijack training. Others describe his hunt for materials to build a radioactive “dirty bomb”.

The documents add little new information about how the attacks were planned, but they do offer a paper trail of accumulating warnings.

Seventy-one presidential daily briefs spanning the period from February 1998 to September 2001. These are the highly classified intelligence summaries prepared for the president and the government’s most senior officials.

The documents run to 101 pages, with the earliest, titled Terrorists seeking WMD capability, dated February 13, 1998.

The last, Situation Report: Bin Laden’s Tracks, is dated September 12, 2001, the day after the attacks.

In between are briefs on the Taliban’s refusal to give bin Laden up, his hunt for chemical, biological and radiological weapons, his financing, and repeated warnings that he intended to strike inside the US.

Many pages are redacted to protect sources.

What did US intelligence know about al-Qaeda before 9/11?

The briefs show that analysts were tracking bin Laden’s movements, the support system around him, his network inside the US and abroad, and how his operations were financed.

Some of the warnings laid out in the presidential briefs were strikingly specific. In September 1998, three years before the attacks, a briefer wrote that bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”.

Analysts also noted his interest in unconventional weapons: Chemical, biological, and radiological.

By June 1999, the briefs included reports that bin Laden’s operatives had experimented with explosives to “increase their energy output”, part of a pursuit of so-called “dirty bombs”.

An April 1998 brief found there was no evidence the Taliban intended to hand bin Laden over, describing him as their “guest” and noting that “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” of Afghanistan between December 1979 and February 1989 left them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.

How many warnings of an attack was the president given?

The warnings weren’t just occasional; they kept coming.

In 1998,1999 and 2000, there were several reports, including one titled Terrorism: Bin Laden Extremists Planning Attacks.

Then in 2001, when George W Bush took over as president from Bill Clinton, the frequency increased, and by the summer the language was increasingly alarming, with one briefing simply titled: Bin Laden Determined To Strike in US.

Did officials know planes could be used in an attack?

A brief dated September 10 that year, titled Bin Ladin’s Location and Intentions, recorded his stated preference for striking Washington, then added that the group behind that summer’s East Africa US embassy bombings “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) had quickly determined that those attacks had been carried out by al-Qaeda.

The same memo cautioned that intelligence gave “no conclusive information” on his intentions for future attacks.

That December, another brief described conspirators who “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and noted that “some members of the Bin Laden network have received hijack training.”

That brief, dated December 4, 1998, was titled Bin Laden Preparing To Hijack US Aircraft and Other Attacks.

Does this prove the US government knew 9/11 was coming?

No. It may raise serious questions about why it did not appear to be more prepared, but it does not show any evidence of a lack of will by the government to prevent an attack.

The newly released material reinforces the explanation that intelligence agencies had many pieces of the puzzle but had failed to assemble them into a clear picture in time.

There is no evidence at all to support conspiracy theories about government involvement or that government officials had prior knowledge of the attacks, which have grown in popularity in the US.

No, some of the briefs have been made public before.

The two best-known items were already out. The August 6, 2001 brief, Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US, was declassified in 2004 at the 9/11 Commission’s request.

The broader findings are also known, including that US intelligence had tracked bin Laden’s intentions for years, that aircraft featured in the reporting, and that none of it identified the time, place, method or targets of the eventual plot. The 9/11 Commission set all of this out more than two decades ago.

The release adds the underlying documents, in the briefers’ own words, rather than a commission summary.

articles.title: Kenyan crackdown on foreign traders prompts fear: 'It's like a dog set loose on us'
articles.summary: The authorities have struggled to contain the fallout, as frightened migrants flee the country.
articles.body:
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.

During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.

"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.

"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."

President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.

During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.

Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.

"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."

Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.

Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.

"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.

"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.

In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.

She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.

"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.

In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.

Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.

Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.

Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.

He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.

The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.

The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.

Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.

Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.

The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.

Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.

Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.

He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.

For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."

The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.

Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.

Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.

Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.

He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.

Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".

The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.

In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.

"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.

"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."

Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.

He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".

"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?

"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."

For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.

"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

articles.title: El Niño has broken Atlantic hurricanes. Now the season is breaking records
articles.summary: The natural climate pattern is having a pronounced effect on this hurricane season.
articles.body: No hurricanes have formed in the Atlantic Ocean 103 days into the season, a new record-long wait driven by a beast of an El Niño strangling fledgling storms. Until today, September 11 was the date of the latest first hurricanes — Gustav (2002) and Humberto (2013). Or at least, the latest we know with confidence since 1966, when satellites started tracking hurricanes more accurately. The first hurricane is now more than a month overdue, and there are no prospects for one in the foreseeable future. Thursday marked the statistical peak of the season, and with just five short-lived tropical storms to date, it is now also the least active one since 1950, according to Phil Klotzbach, a hurricane expert with Colorado State University. The only system that made a run at becoming a hurricane was tiny Tropical Storm Edouard on September 1. Edouard was 14 mph shy of hurricane strength and intensifying when it made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border, cutting it off from the Gulf’s warm water fuel. Looking forward, just over 50% of the entire season’s activity typically occurs after September 10, but El Niño will likely have a say in stifling the Atlantic’s final stretch this year. Last year’s first hurricane showed up in mid-August, and three more spun up in the second half of September. The United States managed to avoid a hurricane landfall last year — if the current quiet season repeats that, it’ll be the first back-to-back years without a hurricane landfall since 2009 and 2010. But it’s worth noting that hurricanes can find windows of opportunity to develop even in the most inactive years – and not a single season since 1966 has gone by without one. Most notably, Category 5 Hurricane Andrew’s catastrophic South Florida landfall in August 1992 happened in a season with just seven storms. El Niño’s hurricane shredder September is hurricane season’s peak because storm-fueling warm water is at its most expansive and hottest alongside ripe atmospheric factors. About two to three hurricanes develop this month on average. The results can be dangerous, as 2024’s Helene and 2022’s Ian proved, slamming the US Gulf Coast as Category 4s. Water temperatures are warm enough for hurricanes right now, but El Niño-fueled wind shear, aka tropical-system kryptonite, has soured the situation. Wind shear involves changes in wind speed and direction at different levels of the atmosphere, and it can shred apart anything from budding tropical systems to fully developed hurricanes. The shear has been record-strong this summer across the Atlantic’s so-called main development region, which extends from Africa through the Caribbean, according to Klotzbach. Many storms get their start in this region at the height of the season — mid-August to early October — but this year it’s been nearly shutdown. Tropical Storm Dolly is the only system that has formed in this part of the ocean so far in 2026, and a wall of wind shear ripped it apart just 24 hours later. A few other systems have tried to develop, but were also defeated by shear. El Niño’s storm-killing winds will remain an obstacle for development in hurricane season’s back stretch, though that’s no reason to get complacent. Plus, late-season storms tend to develop closer to the US, including in the Gulf and off the Southeast coast. Those areas tend to be affected less by El Niño’s wind shear, so they’ll be watched closely. And as we’ve already learned this year, it doesn’t take a hurricane-strength system to cause significant impacts, particularly in a warming world making tropical systems wetter. Tropical Storm Arthur’s remnants fueled widespread flooding along the central Gulf Coast in June. Cottonport, Louisiana, was drenched by 29.06 inches of rain in 24 hours, which obliterated the previous state record of 22 inches set back in 1962. The record is still being reviewed and certified. Heavy rain from Tropical Storm Edouard less than two weeks ago resulted in dangerous flash flooding and water rescues in eastern Texas. A month’s worth of rain fell in an hour and rainfall totals topped 20 inches in some areas north of Beaumont.

Storms can form just about anywhere in the Atlantic basin in September.
Air rises above the warmer Pacific (El Niño conditions), then sinks down over parts of the western Atlantic basin, helping suppress the storms that could grow into a tropical system.
The sinking air over the western half of the Atlantic basin, coupled with increased wind shear, is what tamps down tropical activity during El Niño.

articles.title: Deprogrammed: The 'radical perspective change' that led this transgender atheist to Jesus
articles.summary: Haley Furst lived as a transgender atheist man who supported communism before a coworker reading Romans 8:38 sparked her return to Christian faith.
articles.body: Sitting in the comfort of her sunlit white room, adorned with gold jewelry sits Haley Furst, a woman who identified as a transgender, atheist man who supported communism for several years before rekindling her belief in Jesus Christ. "I believed in anarchal communism, I was an atheist for a moment of my life, and I really believed in whatever the furthest left-leaning political stance one could possibly take, [even from] abortion all the way up until the point of giving birth," Furst told Fox News Digital. "I really just had a radical perspective change where now… I believe in biblical values and everything that entails and what that looks like," she continued. BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS Furst, who grew up in Alberta, Canada, which she described as "the most right-wing" and "conservative leaning" province within the country, detailed the "culture shock" she experienced within her own homeland. "Growing up in a Christian home and having gone to a private Christian school up until high school - first going into that Canadian public high school was very [much a] culture shock… Gender liberation, sexual liberation, [was] a huge topic of conversation at the time [and] what we call GSAs, that's Gay Straight Alliance clubs, within schools," she added. "It was very interesting going from a school where none of those things were discussed, and if they were discussed, it was from a healthy standpoint of, you know, this is what's age-appropriate to talk with teenagers about into a public school. Where [now] this [was] not only talked about in almost every class, but these conversations are had with adult teachers and underage students," Furst continued. PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME As for how this affected her life, she revealed that it led to "about five or six years" during which she "identified as a transgender man." "I was born a female… but for five or six years I presented as a male [and] took male hormones so that I could appear as a man. I had one transitional surgery and that looked [like] a hysterectomy, where they took my uterus and one of my ovaries," she said. Furst said that a coworker who read Romans 8:38 to her was the catalyst for her reignited faith in God that dismantled the worldview she once defended. Romans 8:38-39 reads, "For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD "I had gone home and continued to wrestle with that and by myself alone in my bedroom I said…I'm just going to pray and see what happens, and I highly doubt that Jesus would still want me, but I'm going to do that anyway," Furst continued. "It was a slow heart work, but now I get to come as the woman that I am today, because it was [a] slow and steady journey of [my] relationship with Jesus," she relayed. Furst went on to detail her changed perspective on adults who "share about their sexual identity with children", citing that she is "very critical" of those who choose to have those conversations with those who are underage – especially since she claims early exposure to those conversations were "slowly manipulating her" into struggling with an identity that she never had before. Furst went on to detail her changed perspective on adults who "share about their sexual identity with children," saying she is "very critical" of those who choose to have those conversations with minors — especially since she said early exposure to those conversations was "slowly manipulating her" into struggling with an identity that she never had before. DOJ INVESTIGATES ILLINOIS SCHOOLS OVER SECRET GENDER TRANSITIONS, IDEOLOGY "As someone who had an early childhood where those conversations were very healthy and they were age-appropriate to then going into my teenage years where, at my public Canadian high school it was so talked about in such in-depth detail, you can very much see how that's actually damaging," Furst shared. "There is so much talk, way more talk with children about sexual identity than there ever was in past years where we're having conversations way younger than it needs to be. And I think that parents have [a] very interesting sort of situation now of, how do you navigate keeping your child innocent in a world that tells them the safest thing is for them to know about all these sexual things from a very young age," she stated. "If someone wants to be asking specific details about same-sex sexual actions, I don't think that is age-appropriate for a 13-year-old, 14-year-old. And I also really don't think that that conversation is meant to be had teacher to student. I think that should be reserved for families to decide how they want to approach those conversations and when it's most appropriate for those to be had," Furst said. articles.title: Uganda buries onetime ‘boy king’ whose death has sparked a succession battle
articles.summary: The funeral was underway Saturday in western Uganda for a traditional monarch who ascended the throne of the Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995 and died last month at 34, triggering a succession dispute that has rocked the royal family and gripped the entire nation.
articles.body: KAMPALA, Uganda — The funeral was underway Saturday in western Uganda for a traditional monarch who ascended the throne of the Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995 and died last month at 34, triggering a succession dispute that has rocked the royal family and gripped the entire nation. The funeral of Tooro’s King Oyo Nyimba in a cathedral in the remote city of Fort Portal, near the Congo border, concludes a nine-day mourning period that was blemished by an increasingly acrimonious dispute over who should succeed him. He will be buried next to his ancestors later on Saturday. King Oyo, as he was best known to his subjects, was unmarried when he died late in August after suffering from cancer. Elders with the kingdom’s ruling clan, known as the Babiito, said he never declared an heir to them, disputing the account of others in the kingdom who said he left behind a son born out of wedlock. The son has not been publicly identified, leading to sensational claims on social media of at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo’s children. On Wednesday, a committee of Tooro elders announced that they had chosen a prince working as a journalist to succeed Oyo, earning praise from traditionalists who want an adult on the throne and rebuke from the king’s closest relatives. Oyo’s sister, Ruth Komuntale, said the announcement sought to “bring division and turmoil.” Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death. “I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said in a statement. “Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo.” Traditional monarchs are beloved but don’t wield any formal power in the East African country. Oyo was crowned in 1995, at the age of 3, after his father’s death. He was a curious child in colorful robes and an object of adoration for his hundreds of thousands of followers. At his coronation, he went through a series of tribal rituals and was led into the royal cemetery to perform a coming-of-age ceremony: successfully tossing nine coffee beans into his father’s tomb. Amid the ongoing succession dispute, it was not clear who would perform this rite. The matter of Oyo’s successor could go to the courts, after his family said he left behind a will that had been ignored by Tooro elders. Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest king, a mesmerizing figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela. Oyo was guided by regents appointed by the kingdom until he became an adult at 18. “This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, said in a eulogy posted on social platform X. “Not Oyo; not that likeable young man; not at 34. That’s what makes it so painful.” The late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi befriended the Tooro royal family as if they were part of his extended family. He made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for years before his death in October 2011. Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country, but they were restored in 1993. Although they have no political authority and are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics, monarchs wield authority as guardians of tribal culture.
