articles.title: Saudi Arabia shuts critical oil pipeline after drone attack: What it means
articles.summary: Baghdad launches investigation, closes border after confirming strike came from Iraqi territory.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has temporarily closed its critical East-West oil pipeline, a 1,200km (746-mile) conduit stretching across the Arabian Peninsula, after it was attacked by drones on Friday.

The drones were reported to have been launched from Iraq, where an investigation is under way. No group has claimed responsibility for the strikes so far.

Plumes of smoke from a section of the pipeline could be seen on video footage from the area. It is understood that equipment used to operate the pipeline was also hit.

The closure of the pipeline has halted the flow of Saudi oil exports, which have also been disrupted by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March. A critical artery for the kingdom’s energy exports, it has become all the more important due to the US-Israel war on Iran.

The closure of its pipeline comes as Saudi Arabia is drawn into a new front in the Middle East conflict in Yemen, where Houthi forces have made rapid advances along the coast against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and seized the strategic island of Mayun in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Here’s what we know about the closure of Saudi’s East-West pipeline and what it means for global energy security:

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday said the East-West oil pipeline, which crosses the country from Saudi’s Abqaiq oilfield in the east to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, had been hit in the Riyadh and Medina areas by drones, causing injuries and damage.

The pipeline, which is operated by the majority state-owned Saudi Aramco, has been temporarily shut as a “precaution”, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy. Specialised teams have begun steps to “secure the pipeline and assess its safety”, the ministry said.

Where did the drone attack come from and who launched it?

The attack originated in the southeastern Iraqi province of Maysan, according to the office of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.

No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, and neither Saudi Arabia nor the Iraqi government have publicly identified a group they suspect of being behind it.

Iraq is home to numerous Iran-backed armed groups, however.

Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s oil pipeline had most likely been carried out by one of these groups.

“I believe this [attack] was most likely an order from Tehran. From Tehran’s point of view, this is them supporting Yemen’s Houthi war objective, which is for Saudi Arabia to withdraw from Yemen,” he said.

Iran-backed groups are calculating that the more pressure Saudi Arabia feels from attacks on its territory, the more likely it is to withdraw from Yemen, where the Houthi rebels fighting the internationally recognised government are backed by Iran, said Pusztai.

“On the other side, this certainly sharpens Iran’s own blockade over the Strait of Hormuz because Tehran does not allow Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz any more. This signals to Saudi Arabia – and probably to the other Gulf states – that Iran can’t be trusted.”

The Iraqi government formally condemned the attack, saying it does not accept its territory being used as a “launchpad for attacks against any nation” and that it would take “legal action against anyone proven to be involved”.

Iraq’s prime minister has ordered a probe into the Maysan operations command, which oversees security in the province Baghdad says the attack came from, and has dismissed its commander.

Iraq has also ordered the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing between Iraq and Iran as a precautionary measure, two security sources told Reuters on Saturday.

So far, Saudi Arabia has opted not to retaliate. In a statement, the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it would hold off on responding “at this stage” at the request of the Iraqi prime minister.

However, Riyadh said it reserves the right to “take ⁠all measures necessary” to protect its interests.

In July, the United States and Saudi Arabia launched joint attacks on the Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) in Iraq, killing at least 20 members of the group, after Saudi Arabia claimed it launched drone attacks on its oil facilities.

Iraq’s National Security Council, chaired by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, called the attacks on the PMF bases in seven Iraqi provinces “a flagrant violation of Iraq’s sovereignty and the sanctity of its lands”.

Abdulaziz Alghashian, a senior nonresident fellow at the Gulf International Forum think tank, said Saudi Arabia, which recently signed a defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan , is likely to eventually retaliate, possibly in coordination with other regional allies.

Alghashian told Al Jazeera that he would not expect much from the Saudi-Turkiye-Pakistan Mecca defence pact announced in August, for now, as it is “still under construction”, but that there could still be some form of “multilateral response”.

“I think we’re going to see more escalation in the region and more military confrontation,” said Alghashian. “The question is just the extent of it”.

How significant is the closure of this pipeline?

The East-West pipeline has ⁠been moving four million to five million barrels of oil per day (bpd) in recent months, amounting to 4 to 5 percent of global supply, according to data cited by Reuters. It had increased capacity specifically to help mitigate the disruption to Saudi oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz.

While oil exports remain far below normal in the conflict-hit Strait of Hormuz, the closure of the East-West pipeline is expected to create more pain for global energy, as US diesel prices hit an all-time high and Brent crude oil – the global benchmark – currently costs more than $104 per barrel, say analysts.

Before the US-Israeli war on Iran commenced on February 28, Brent crude was trading at about $72 per barrel. Early in the conflict, it hit a high of $119.

“This is a real blow,” Ben Cahill, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council Global Energy Center, told Al Jazeera, referring to the pipeline as Saudi Arabia’s “principal bypass option to avoid the Strait of Hormuz”.

“The key buffers that got us through the last six months have basically been worn away,” he said.

Saudi political analyst Khalid Bartafi told Al Jazeera that the attacks on the pipeline could cause a crisis for the global community.

“It’s going to be very dire consequences because we are talking about five million barrels of oil for export disappearing from the market,” he said. “The next 48 will tell you whether this is going to remain some sort of contained incident or this is going to become yet another major regional escalation.”

He added: “This is not just our problem, it’s a global problem because if Iran could close both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb the world will pay. The world community needs to do something.”

How quickly can the pipeline be reopened?

After a pumping station on the same pipeline was struck in April, causing output to fall to 700,000bpd, Saudi Arabia announced it had been repaired and restored to full capacity just three days later.

However, Saudi Arabia has not provided details on the extent of the damage from the latest attack. Satellite images showed smoke emerging from an area of the pipeline south of Medina. NASA also detected unusual thermal activity in the area.

What other options does Saudi Arabia have for its oil exports?

None that can readily compensate for the loss of the pipeline.

With exports hugely restricted in the Strait of Hormuz, the East-West pipeline had served as Saudi Arabia’s main bypass route, bringing crude oil from eastern Saudi Arabia westward to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

That means Saudi Arabia cannot simply redirect the same eastern crude to Yanbu while the pipeline is shut. Meanwhile, it can try to make greater use of existing stocks in the west, but the Houthis’ newfound control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and Mayun island, also known as Perim island, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait could pose further challenges to getting that oil out – even if longer journeys around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope are viable.

As a result, Saudi Arabia will likely reroute more exports through Egypt via the Suez Canal or the Sumed pipeline, a 320km (199-mile) pipeline carrying crude oil from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean Sea.

Cahill added that the closure of the East-West pipeline could have ripple effects across an already squeezed global energy market.

“There’s less slack in the system, everything is running hot,” said Cahill. If attacks continue and there is “any real threat that the Red Sea is going to be cut off for some time”, he added, it would mean further upward pressure on prices.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow as Yemen hits back against Houthis
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, with the latest squeeze reverberating through the region Saturday as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, with the latest squeeze reverberating through the region Saturday as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis. The 745-mile pipeline had helped Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude oil exporter, bypass the blocked Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass before the U.S. and Israel waged war on Iran in late February. The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline on Friday, adding that drone attacks had resulted in a number of injuries and that its teams were “taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.” Saudi Arabia said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement. The pipeline has been moving 4-5% of global oil supplies, new agency Reuters reported Friday. An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq‘s prime minister’s office. Iraq also closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq’s state-run news agency reported Saturday. Kuwait, a U.S. ally in the region, warned that the pipeline attack was a “dangerous escalation that undermines the security and stability of the region,” while Bahrain stressed Saudi Arabia’s right to “take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty.” U.S. President Donald Trump said on ⁠Saturday that everything would “work out just ⁠fine” when asked about the region on a visit to Ireland. He also said, without providing evidence, that Iran was “probably” behind the pipeline attack. The pipeline strikes came as rebel Houthi forces in Yemen captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, which serves as a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia. The Houthis also captured the historic port city of Mocha this week, followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government from Perim, also known as Mayun. If the Houthis are able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway. Saudi Arabia has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz. Yemeni Ministry of Defense said Saturday it had carried out counterattacks against Houthi targets, hitting militants, vehicles and weaponry. A statement issued by Houthi forces on Friday said that “maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels,” vowing to strike Saudi targets “until the aggression stops and the blockade against our dear people is lifted.” Trump said the Houthis had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.” Oil prices ended the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since Mid-May after the dramatic developments. Effective Houthi control over the Red Sea coast “is a game changer,” and could give Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States, Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News. He said: “Far from being really besieged and bleeding, Iran now could easily increase the pain to the U.S. economy and the world economy.” Gerges said it remains to be seen whether the Houthis can maintain their control of the vast areas of the Red Coast, or if they “overextended themselves.” But the Trump administration “now finds itself in a much more difficult position because it gambled that the blockade of Iran would force Iran to accept Trump’s conditions,” he added. “The reverse has happened.” Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian said Saturday that it would sign an agreement with Oman over a joint route through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, as part of a deal securing future navigation rights through the strait. That deal is not expected to immediately reopen the waterway without a broader agreement with the U.S., Iran has previously stressed. The U.S. military is helping its Saudi counterparts to develop and coordinate targets inside Yemen, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the matter, after Saudi Arabia vowed a firm response to hostilities. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman is urging President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, according to a person familiar with the matter. The president and the Crown Prince have discussed the recent escalation by the Houthis at least twice in the last 24 hours, this person said Friday. The United Nations’ International Organization for Migration warned on Friday at least 46,000 people have so far been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week. It said that figure spanned the West Coast and Taiz governorates as of Thursday, with the numbers of those displaced “alarmingly rising by the hour.” The organization called on all parties to the conflict to “guarantee safe humanitarian access and to protect civilians, aid workers and assets on the ground.”

articles.title: Man in court following anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
articles.summary: Del Leon Somerville, 42, is accused of throwing a bottle and kicking out at a police officer.
articles.body:
A man accused of throwing a bottle at police during disorder at an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth has appeared in court.

Police attended Eastney Marina on 6 September after hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

Del Leon Somerville, 42, from Paulsgrove appeared at Portsmouth Magistrates Court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police officer.

He was remanded in custody to appear at Portsmouth Crown Court on 16 September.

Somerville did not enter any plea during his appearannce.

Prosecutor Lucy Paddick told the court he was accused of throwing a bottle towards a police line during the protests.

He was also allegedly heard shouting an expletive as the bottle was thrown.

Somerville was also accused of kicking out at a police officer, making contact with his right thigh.

Groups from South Coast Patriots are expected to demonstrate in Portsmouth city centre later, and Stand Up To Racism to host a counter protest.

Hampshire Police has warned that protesters wearing face coverings could face arrest.

The force said it would use the powers under the Crime and Policing Act 2025 to "allow peaceful protest and prevent violence".

The powers will apply to anyone involved in protests within a map area designated by police between 10:00 BST Saturday and 10:00 Sunday.

Staffordshire Police also said it would ban the use of face coverings at a planned protest in Tamworth on Saturday, where Britain First has said it will carry out a so-called March for Remigration.

Northumbria Police has a similar ban in place in Newcastle city centre.

Hampshire Police previously said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption in Eastney, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

articles.title: Why Erika Kirk’s forgiveness matters
articles.summary: Author William P. Young says Erika Kirk's public forgiveness of Charlie Kirk's assassin powerfully illustrates his new book "Return to the Shack."
articles.body: Author William P. Young’s new book "Return to the Shack" centers on the power of forgiveness, and he praised Erika Kirk for presenting a strong display of it last year. Young’s novel "The Shack" tells the story of a father’s healing process after his daughter was kidnapped and killed on a camping trip. The grieving dad, Mack, receives a mysterious letter from God asking him to come to a shack, where he meets an unorthodox Holy Trinity. While considered controversial by some religious readers, the story largely resonated with audiences and was turned into a motion picture in 2017. Young's sequel focuses on forgiveness as Mack comes face-to-face with his daughter’s killer as he is given a more humanized storyline. "I think we need to make a distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation," Young told Fox News Digital. "Forgiveness is for the sake of the one who's been harmed, so that you can continue to live your life without the specter of what's on your shoulders. And I mean, you can forgive someone and never trust them again. Reconciliation is the slow, arduous, painful process of learning how to trust. Or taking the risk that you might become trustworthy if you've done the harm. So, reconciliation is for the sake of the perpetrator, much more than forgiveness is." ‘THE SHACK’ AUTHOR EXPECTS MORE CHRISTIAN CRITICISM WITH SEQUEL, BUT WILL TAKE IT IN STRIDE Making peace is essential, he said. "Otherwise, you're going to live with a corpse of an event or a situation or some human being who may be dead," he continued. "A lot of abuse was done to us by people who no longer are alive. And if we can't let them go, which is the idea of forgiveness, is that we move our hands from around their throat so that we may hold something other than their throat, like life. And it becomes essential. Otherwise, we're poisoning all the relationships around us." Erika Kirk, the widow of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, shocked many Americans when she publicly forgave the man accused of assassinating her husband last year. Kirk was killed while speaking at a Turning Point USA event one year ago at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. "Our Savior said, 'Father, forgive them, for they not know what they do,'" Erika said at her husband's memorial service. "That young man … I forgive him. I forgive him because it was what Christ did, and it's what Charlie would do." Young found it a very powerful example of the message he’s trying to convey. ERIKA KIRK FORGIVES HUSBAND'S KILLER AT MEMORIAL SERVICE: ‘IT’S WHAT CHARLIE WOULD DO' "And I think that's what Erika was doing, saying, ‘I'm not going to let what you have done to own me,'" the author said. "I'm not going to enter the same prison that you are now in,’ metaphorically, of course." "And so, in terms of the human journey, we have this — same with every guy on death row — they don't have, in the deepest places of their heart, a desire to be harmful or to be non-truth tellers or to be unkind," Young continued. "They're human beings and that raises a question is why should that be the deepest places of movement towards a wholeness of what it means to be human by saying, ‘I want to do the work, what it takes to not be addicted. To be a truth-teller, to be someone who is kind and caring.’" "And part of that is the underlying belief that love is actually more powerful than violence, or love is more powerful than harm," he added. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION ‘THE SHACK’ AUTHOR EXPECTS MORE CHRISTIAN CRITICISM WITH SEQUEL, BUT WILL TAKE IT IN STRIDEYoung said that is often not the reality and not everyone takes the route Kirk took. "And we live in a world where it seems like violence is really the power," he said. "In word, thought, or deed, whether we're using it in words online, or we're perpetrating it to the person in front of us, or we're gossiping about someone in order to give ourselves a boost and them a detraction. Love is more powerful, and that's my statement. You know, that's, I'm solidly convinced that it is, because it actually changes things." Young couldn’t discuss the art of making amends without reflecting on his own years-long journey to forgive his father. "Violence doesn't change any things," he said. "It only adds to the violence that already exists. And, you know, my dad was an abusive man when I was growing up. And if I thought that treating him with violence was going to be a resolution, I would have been absolutely blind and ignorant." "It's not violence," Young added. "It's care. It's love. It's listening. It's that people shouldn't take a timeout, and the state offers one if you don't adhere to the rules. But even then, I think that love, God, meets us where we're at and begins to move us in a direction toward our wholeness so that we can learn to love others, and we can learn to love ourselves, and that produces incredible outcomes that would not be available otherwise." articles.title: NIA raids 10 locations across Jammu & Kashmir in LeT-linked terror conspiracy case
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Saturday conducted searches at 10 locations across Jammu and Kashmir in connection with a cross-.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Saturday conducted searches at 10 locations across Jammu and Kashmir in connection with a cross-border terror conspiracy involving Pakistan-based handlers of the proscribed Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and their alleged network of local Over Ground Workers (OGWs).The searches were carried out in Kupwara, Kulgam, Bandipora, Baramulla and Sopore to gather further evidence related to the conspiracy and ascertain the roles of individuals allegedly providing logistical and other support to infiltrated terrorists, the NIA said.During the searches, incriminating material relevant to the case was seized or secured, according to the agency. The material is being examined and corroborated with other evidence collected during the investigation.Investigation began with OGW arrestThe case was initially registered at Police Station Zakoora in Srinagar and was subsequently re-registered by the NIA under Section 23 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, Sections 7 and 25 of the Arms Act, 1959, and Section 4 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908.The investigation began after the arrest of an alleged LeT-linked OGW at a naka point during the night of March 31, 2026. A hand grenade and live ammunition were recovered from his possession, the NIA said.Further investigation led to the arrest of Pakistani nationals allegedly linked to the conspiracy and helped investigators identify the suspected roles of members of the local support network.According to the NIA, the investigation so far has revealed links between Pakistan-based LeT handlers and their local associates. These associates were allegedly being used for communication, movement and concealment of infiltrated terrorists, as well as providing shelter, conducting reconnaissance and facilitating other logistical requirements.NIA examines financial, communication trailsThe agency is also examining the financial trail, communication channels and movement of the accused, along with the source and supply chain of arms and explosives.The objective, according to the NIA, is to establish the complete network and determine the extent of its activities.The latest searches are part of the agency's continuing investigation into the larger conspiracy and the support mechanism allegedly facilitating cross-border terrorism.The NIA said it would continue its investigation to identify all persons involved in the alleged conspiracy and establish their respective roles. Further legal action, including arrests and recoveries, may follow depending on the outcome of the investigation.Hafiz Saeed warrant in related terror caseThe searches come amid the NIA's wider investigations into LeT-linked terror networks in Jammu and Kashmir.A Special Court in Jammu on September 8 issued a non-bailable warrant against LeT founder Hafiz Saeed in a terror case related to the alleged supply of weapons, funds and directions to terror groups operating in the Union Territory.It was the second non-bailable warrant issued against Saeed by the Special NIA Court in Jammu in two months.The warrant was issued after the NIA described Saeed, a resident of Sargodha in Pakistan's Punjab province, as an “absconding accused” in a case concerning the arrest of Mohammad Naqeeb Bhat during a check at Pandach on the outskirts of Srinagar earlier this year.A China-made grenade and 15 live rounds were recovered from Bhat, who was booked under the UAPA, Arms Act and Explosive Substances Act.The subsequent investigation led to the alleged busting of a terror network and the arrest of several more terrorists associated with LeT and its offshoot The Resistance Front (TRF), as well as two Pakistani nationals.The NIA told the court that Saeed was allegedly operating from Pakistan and providing weapons, money and directions to terrorists in the Kashmir Valley.The court observed that Saeed's involvement had surfaced during the investigation and that he was “allegedly involved in terrorism”.The latest warrant followed an earlier non-bailable warrant issued against him on July 8 in connection with the Pahalgam terror attack case.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Israel-Lebanon talks postponed as explosions rock southern Lebanon
articles.summary: President Aoun says ‘no new negotiations with Israel at the moment’.
articles.body:
The next round of United States-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon has been postponed as Israeli forces continue to strike and demolish buildings across southern Lebanon.

In a sudden visit to the war-stricken southern city of Nabatieh on Saturday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun confirmed that “there will be no new negotiations with Israel at the moment.

“Withdrawal, the return of prisoners and displaced people, and reconstruction are national principles that we pledge to implement,” he was quoted as saying.

Earlier, the AFP news agency quoted an unnamed US official as saying the next round of talks scheduled for this month in Rome will not be happening until October.

The Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors will instead meet at the Department of State next week to discuss the continued implementation of a framework agreement announced in June, the official said.

Under that agreement, the Lebanese army would disarm Hezbollah in so-called “pilot zones”. The Lebanese armed group has rejected direct talks with Israel.

On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz issued a joint statement pledging their forces would remain in southern Lebanon, to stop Hezbollah re-establishing its presence there.

The same day, Israeli forces detonated 1,100 tonnes of explosives at what they claimed was a Hezbollah central command complex built into the Ali al-Taher Ridge, causing tremors throughout surrounding areas in southern Lebanon.

Nabatieh, which sits below the ridge, has been a strategic flashpoint in the war that Israel says it has gained operational control over after weeks of fighting.

Israeli attacks in the area have killed at least 29 people in the last two weeks, including 12 members of the same family in an air raid on Kfar Ramman, which neighbours Nabatieh.

On Saturday, heavy explosions shook the town of al-Mansouri, heard and felt as far as Tyre and its surrounding areas, Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) reported. Israeli artillery also shelled the Douha area of Kfar Reman, the outskirts of Arnoun and Wadi al-Salouqi.

A day earlier, Israeli forces blew up most of al-Mansouri’s public school, leaving a small section standing, and carried out a two-wave air raid on Nabatieh al-Fawqa, NNA reported. Israeli drones also flew low over Beirut and its southern suburbs.

The reports added that Israeli forces had begun demolishing homes using drones to drop barrels of explosive material on roofs.

articles.title: Trail honours generations of Devon shipyard workers
articles.summary: A new Shipyard Trail between Bideford and Appledore highlights more than 500 years of shipbuilding.
articles.body:
Routes used by generations of workers travelling to and from historic shipyards are being celebrated with a special trail.

The new Shipyard Trail gives visitors the chance to follow the routes between Bideford and Appledore yards in north Devon and highlights more than 500 years of shipbuilding along the Torridge estuary.

The launch on 19 September forms part of a wider programme for the Heritage Open Days 2026 in Devon , and celebrates "the everyday histories of working lives", said organisers English Heritage.

Heritage Open Days are also being held in Cornwall and, separately, National Trust Jersey is holding an open day on 19 September .

The trail links locations where vessels ranging from wooden fishing boats to Royal Navy ships and modern military craft were built, many of which have little visible evidence of their industrial past today, but shaped communities on both sides of the river.

Ahead of the launch, an exhibition from 17 to 19 September at the Pannier Pantry on Bridgeland Street in Barnstaple will showcase the Shipyard Trail, the Young Shipwrights Project 2026 and the restoration of the lifeboat Jane Hannah MacDonald III.

Other events include tours of the Steamship Freshspring and a special open day celebrating the history of Bridgeland Street.

Daniel Defoe, author of Robinson Crusoe, visiting in 1724, described Bridgeland Street as a "spacious, broad, well-built street inhabited with wealthy merchants who trade to most parts of the trading world".

A number of events are also being held in Cornwall to mark Heritage Open Days including a guided tour at Chysauster ancient village and Bodmin materials recycling centre.

National Trust Jersey is marking Heritage Open Day by opening the doors to four properties on 19 September, La Ronde Porte in St Saviour, Sous les Bois in Trinity, Le Moulin de Quétivel in St Peter and the Georgian House in St Helier.

articles.title: Trump says Iran likely responsible for attack on vital Saudi oil pipeline
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has said that Iran was most likely behind the attack on a vital oil pi
articles.body: US President Donald Trump said Iran was “probably” behind the attack on a vital oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia which led to its closure. The East-West Pipeline was attacked by several drones coming from Iraq on Thursday, the Saudi foreign ministry said Friday, resulting in injuries and some damage. The energy ministry added that the pipeline had been shut down as a precautionary measure. The news comes amid turmoil in energy markets and major disruption in shipping with no end in sight to the Iran war and as Tehran’s allies in Yemen, the Houthis, seized a key island and a port in the Red Sea. Trump pointed the finger at Iran as most likely being behind the attack when asked about the incident by a reporter during a visit to Ireland on Saturday. “I think they are, probably they are,” Trump told journalists in Dublin. It remains unclear at this stage who was behind the attacks. A key umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq, known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, has denied responsibility. The attack is another headache for Saudi Arabia, which has been backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis. Trump said he had held a call with Saudi Crown ​Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he referred to ​as ‌a “good friend.” A source told CNN that the Saudi Crown Prince had spoken twice with Trump on Thursday and urged him to strike the Houthis as the Iran-backed group advances towards the Red Sea, but Trump declined. Responding to a question about the fresh concerns in Saudi Arabia following the closure of the pipeline, and whether he could help move marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in light of the developments, Trump said everything will “work out fine.” The White House, in response to CNN’s questions about the calls, said that the US was in touch with the Saudis and “focused on protecting our core national security interests— such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges.” Borders close in Iraq Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy statement said the pipeline “was subjected to multiple attacks” on Thursday that “resulted in a number of injuries.” The statement added that teams were “taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.” The Iraqi government condemned the attacks, saying it had ordered an urgent investigation into those responsible and that it will not allow its territory or airspace to be used for such purposes. On Saturday, Iraqi authorities said the country has closed a number of its borders as a precautionary measure. The strike and recent Houthi advances along the Red Sea signal that Saudi Arabia’s oil resources — and its ability to export those resources — are facing increasing threats as the Iran war continues. Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline has become vital for the country to maintain oil exports since the outbreak of the US-Iran war. The kingdom has rerouted about 5 million barrels of oil per day that would have been destined for awaiting oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, as Iran effectively shuttered the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, that oil has traveled through the pipeline to Saudi Arabia’s port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: In 2001, a security guard led 6 people trapped on the 70th floor to safety as the World Trade Center burned; 25 years later, the survivors he saved are trying to save his life
articles.summary: US News: When the World Trade Center was engulfed in smoke and flames on September 11, 2001, a security guard carrying a flashlight and bullhorn appeared to si.
articles.body: When the World Trade Center was engulfed in smoke and flames on September 11, 2001, a security guard carrying a flashlight and bullhorn appeared to six people who were struggling to find a way out of the South Tower. He was Dereck Lovell, who was filling in that day and had never previously worked on their floor. Lovell guided the group towards a functioning staircase, helping them escape from a building that would collapse minutes later. Nearly 25 years on, the man those survivors credit with saving their lives is facing a different fight. In interviews with PEOPLE, Doug Brown recalled how Lovell helped the group escape, while Lovell revealed that he is battling kidney cancer and now needs a transplant.A chance assignment on a day that changed everythingLovell, now 68, was working as a security guard at the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. He had been filling in as a security guard on the 70th floor of the South Tower when the second hijacked plane struck the building. The impact sent Lovell flying from his chair towards an elevator. He suffered a shoulder injury but was able to continue helping people evacuate. As smoke spread through the tower, he carried a flashlight and bullhorn while directing workers towards a usable staircase.Among those searching for an escape route were Doug Brown and five colleagues from Morgan Stanley. Brown, who was then an associate national sales director, recalled that the group was surrounded by smoke, flames and collapsing ceilings. The stairways they knew about had been destroyed, leaving the group disoriented. Visibility was so poor that Brown could see only about an arm's length ahead. Then he heard Lovell's voice.“Follow me,” the security guard told them, according to Brown's recollection. Lovell led the six people to a staircase only about 15 feet away. Brown had never known the stairwell was there and initially mistook it for a broom closet. That small discovery became critical to their survival.The guard kept helping even after finding an escape routeLovell did not simply direct Brown and his colleagues towards the stairs and leave. After helping the group get into the stairwell, he continued searching the floor and found three more employees whom he also guided towards safety before beginning his own descent.For Brown, the encounter remained one of the defining moments of his life. “If Dereck hadn't been there,” Brown told PEOPLE, “I think best-case scenario we would've had dumb luck and found that stairwell.” Brown and his colleagues later managed to identify the security guard who had helped them. Days after the attacks, they tracked Lovell down and invited him to Morgan Stanley's temporary offices in Jersey City, New Jersey, where they thanked him personally.Lovell recalled the meeting, saying that everyone hugged him and thanked him. The connection between Lovell and Brown did not end that day. The two have remained in contact for almost 25 years.A second rescue unfolded during the escapeBrown's own journey to safety also involved another life-saving act. While descending the tower, Brown and a colleague encountered Silvion Ramsundar, an investment executive who had been on the 78th floor. Ramsundar was severely wounded and covered in blood. The two survivors fashioned a makeshift compress from a handkerchief to slow the bleeding from a wound near his heart. They then helped Ramsundar descend roughly 60 floors before reaching an ambulance, only minutes before the South Tower collapsed.Doctors later found that a piece of metal about the size of a playing card had lodged near Ramsundar's aorta. He also suffered a broken collarbone and a collapsed lung. Ramsundar has previously told PEOPLE that he remains grateful to Brown for helping him survive that morning. The stories of Lovell, Brown and Ramsundar illustrate how survival on September 11 often depended on strangers helping one another amid conditions that were changing by the minute.Nearly 25 years later, Lovell needs helpThe relationship between Lovell and Brown has taken on a new meaning as the 25th anniversary of the attacks approaches. According to PEOPLE, Lovell was diagnosed with kidney cancer last September. He had previously battled prostate cancer that he believed was connected to his exposure to 9/11 toxins.In 2026, both of Lovell's kidneys were removed. He now undergoes dialysis three days a week while waiting for a kidney transplant. Lovell is listed as a transplant candidate through SUNY Downstate and NYU Langone. He said the waiting process could take years unless a suitable donor can be found through another route.Now Brown is trying to help the man he credits with helping him survive one of the darkest days in American history. He is raising awareness of Lovell's need for a kidney donor and encouraging people to learn about his situation. Lovell, however, remains modest about what happened in the South Tower. Despite the gratitude of the people he helped, Lovell does not describe himself as a hero. “I did my job that day,” he said.Brown sees it differently. Nearly a quarter-century after Lovell appeared through the smoke with a flashlight and led his group towards a hidden staircase, Brown still believes the security guard gave him the chance to keep living. For Brown, the man who helped him escape the burning World Trade Center was more than a security guard doing his job. He was, as Brown put it, a “guardian angel”. Now, after all these years, the survivors Lovell once helped are hoping they can return the favour.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Left with nothing, people in Gaza are forced to rent generators by the hour
articles.summary: Israel’s destruction of homes and infrastructure in Gaza has forced Palestinians to rent generators by the hour.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – For more than four hours, Hajj Rabhi al-Fairi, 79, has been standing outside his home in Gaza City with his children and neighbours waiting their turn to use a small generator.

The generator’s owner pours in the fuel, starts a timer and switches on the machine.

Each family gets a few minutes to operate a pump that pushes water up to a storage tank on the roof, before the generator moves on to the next house.

For al-Fairi and his neighbours, this is how they get water.

“We have an old water pump, but there is no electricity to run it. We have to rent a generator,” al-Fairi tells Al Jazeera.

Since the family returned to their home in October 2025, after fleeing a month earlier during Israel’s assault on their neighbourhood, the generator has become a familiar sight on the streets of Nassr.

When it arrives, residents gather around it, each carrying a jerrycan of diesel to operate the machine, which they have to pay for themselves.

“We came back and found the place a tragedy,” he says.

Their neighbourhood and home were badly damaged from years of Israeli bombing, with no municipal electricity or water supplies functioning. The family depends on an old pump – but without electricity, it cannot bring water up to the rooftop tank.

Each family needs only about seven or eight minutes to fill up their tanks, but with the number of flats in their building, the generator needs to be rented for about an hour.

The cost has also risen. Al-Rabhi says families used to pay about 80 to 90 shekels ($26-30) to rent a generator for an hour. At different times, the price has risen to about 100 or 120 shekels ($33-40) an hour, excluding the cost of diesel.

Khalil Abu Ouda, 39, takes a machine mounted on a horse-driven cart from one house to another. The generator’s metal body is covered in black soot and grease, and white smoke rises from the engine when it operates.

At each house, Abu Ouda connects long electrical cables to the water pump. The cables stretch across the street as neighbours gather around the machine to wait their turn.

For Abu Ouda, this machine is both a service for the neighbourhood and an essential source of income for his family.

He says there are very few small, mobile generators, like his, left in working condition in Gaza. Many have broken down, while spare parts are difficult to find or too expensive to source due to Israel’s siege.

Mechanics are also expensive to hire, while fuel and engine oil are increasingly scarce and costly.

“If I could, I would lower the price as much as possible,” he says.

At the same time, demand has never been higher.

“People are under pressure and they need water. If I stayed working until morning, I would keep working,” Abu Ouda says.

To cope with the demand, he often works for 10 to 12 hours a day, putting pressure on himself and the machine.

“But this is our livelihood. There is no alternative,” he said.

With most Palestinians in Gaza having no home or losing their possessions due to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, they have to rent or hire items or services for the most basic household chores.

This includes washing clothes, something once done at home but now impossible to do with no power.

Earlier in the war, Abeer Ghorab, 52, used to wash everything herself. Now she gathers clothes from her tent and takes them to a nearby laundry, where they can be washed and dried in far less time and with less effort.

“When these laundries started opening, they gave us some relief,” Ghorab said.

The difference is particularly important in winter, when heavy clothes, blankets and bedding can take time to dry.

“In winter, the tracksuits are heavy. They need another day to dry,” she said. “When I bring them here, they wash and dry them for me, and I get them back clean and dry. That really helps.”

But due to a limited income, Ghorab cannot afford to use this laundry service every day.

Before the war, Ghorab had a washing machine, a refrigerator and regular electricity at home.

“Things we once took for granted have become dreams. Now we have to pay for every little thing we used to do at home.”

Across Gaza, the infrastructure that once allowed families to carry out everyday tasks at home has been severely disrupted.

A recent United Nations assessment found that 91 percent of surveyed households experienced moderate-to-high water shortages in early August.

A separate damage assessment by the authority found that 107,941 of the 178,632 housing units inspected – about 60 percent – were severely damaged, destroyed or otherwise considered uninhabitable.

Water systems, electricity, sanitation and household appliances, which families relied on to manage daily life, have also been disrupted.

For families living in damaged homes, tents or makeshift shelters, everyday tasks must be paid for.

Fadi Abu Shawarb, 23, has worked at his family’s al-Hurriya laundry for six years.

Before the war, the business relied on large, 50kg (110lb) washing machines for carpets, blankets and other heavy loads. But due to the high cost of operation, these machines are far too expensive to run.

“We started replacing the 50kg machines with 25kg ones because there is not enough electricity,” Fadi says. “There are no solar panels, no reliable power, and the generators are always breaking down.”

Most of his customers are displaced families who lack electricity, water or washing machines at home.

The laundry now handles about 20 to 30 loads a day, with clothes-washing among the most in-demand services.

A load costs six shekels ($2) when the laundry can use solar power and 12 shekels ($4) when it relies on a generator.

But even that is hard for people to pay. “People’s situation is difficult,” he says.

For Ghorab, the laundry is only one of the many expenses she now has to budget for.

“I feel like I’m going through a difficult time,” she says. “I have to pay for every little thing in my day, and with how difficult things are, it’s hard to keep up with everything.”

articles.title: Yemen government forces say Houthi ‘members, vehicles’ targeted in Mocha
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces says they launched air strikes on Houthi fighters along the Red Sea coast.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces say they have launched air strikes on Houthi fighters along the Red Sea coast after the group seized full control of the strategic shoreline.

The country witnessed a sharp military escalation across several fronts on Saturday, particularly along the country’s western coast, as fighting continued with government forces describing the confrontation as a “battle for survival”.

Yemen’s government news agency, Saba, reported that “the armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime” near the port of the city of Mocha.

The spokesperson for the government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they have also struck the Houthis’ “vehicles and members” on the Mocha-Dhubab road, 11km (7 miles) from the city, according to Saba.

The Houthis captured the city of Mocha on Thursday and the island of Mayun on Friday, completing their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a narrow waterway vital to global oil shipping.

Saudi Arabia has temporarily closed its critical East-West oil pipeline, a 1,200km (746-mile) conduit stretching across the Arabian Peninsula, after it was attacked by drones on Friday.

The drones were reported to have been launched from Iraq, where an investigation is under way. No group has claimed responsibility for the strikes so far.

Iraq’s parliament speaker, Haybat al-Halbousi, condemned the use of Iraqi territory for the attack, calling it “unacceptable” and out of step with the country’s policies and its relations with neighbouring states.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman telephoned President Donald Trump twice last week, asking for United States air strikes on the Houthis but was turned down both times, US media outlet Axios earlier reported.

After arriving in Dublin on a two-day visit on Saturday, Trump said the Houthis have asked Washington not to intervene.

“The Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump said. “They don’t want us to go after them.”

The head of US Central Command, which oversees American forces across the Middle East, is now in Saudi Arabia for talks on the advances, a source told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Hull Maritime Museum welcomes 50,000 visitors in first month
articles.summary: The newly restored Hull Maritime Museum reopened on 8 August after a major refurbishment.
articles.body:
Hull Maritime Museum has said the newly restored attraction had 50,000 visitors in its first month.

The museum reopened following a £20m renovation on 8 August.

The museum said there was strong public interest and visitors had travelled from across the region and beyond to see the exhibitions, which celebrate Hull's seafaring past.

Mike Ross, leader of Hull City Council, said the turnout was a "fantastic achievement".

Hull Maritime Museum is a Grade II*-listed landmark dating back to 1871.

The building is the former Dock Offices on Queen Victoria Square, and ships once sailed directly past its doors. It first opened as a museum in 1975.

Following the revamp, the museum said 50% more objects had gone on display, including some from one of Hull's whaling vessels.

The museum said it had already achieved a quarter of its annual target for visitor numbers.

"To welcome more than 50,000 visitors in the museum's first month is a fantastic achievement and demonstrates just how important Hull Maritime Museum is to our city and its communities," Ross said.

articles.title: Arrests after car being driven wrong way down M1 crashes
articles.summary: Police say a man is seriously injured after being hit by the vehicle near Wakefield.
articles.body:
A man has been seriously injured after a car being driven the wrong way hit his vehicle on the M1 near Wakefield.

West Yorkshire Police said a blue Kia Proceed had failed to stop for police and was being driven the wrong way up the northbound carriageway, where it struck a red Dacia Sandero shortly after 23:00 BST on Friday.

The driver of the Dacia, a man in his 20s, was taken to hospital with potentially life-changing injuries.

Three people - an 18-year-old man, a 15-year-old girl and a 30-year-old woman - have been arrested for causing injury by dangerous driving. One other person fled the scene.

The woman was also arrested for being over the prescribed limit.

Anyone who witnessed the crash has been urged to come forward by officers.
